claim: Accumulation of lipid deposits in ectopic tissues is associated with age-associated illnesses including diabetes, hepatic and pancreatic steatoses and other metabolic illnesses that shorten lifespan.
source: On the one hand, accumulation of lipid deposits in ectopic tissues is associated with age-associated illnesses including diabetes, hepatic and pancreatic steatoses and other metabolic illnesses that shorten lifespan (Conte et al., 2019a; Schmeisser et al., 2019; Shulman, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Conte et al., 2019a; Schmeisser et al., 2019; Shulman, 2014).

claim: Converting excess lipid deposits to energy via lipolysis, fatty acid breakdown via beta-oxidation, and increased electron transport chain activity in mitochondria have been proposed to benefit health and longevity.
source: Converting the excess lipid deposits to energy via a cascade of metabolic reactions: lipolysis of triglyceride lipids, fatty acid breakdown via beta-oxidation and increased electron transport chain activity in the mitochondria, have been proposed to benefit health and longevity (Bonawitz et al., 2007; Conte et al., 2019b; Vatner et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bonawitz et al., 2007; Conte et al., 2019b; Vatner et al., 2018).

claim: Increased metabolic activity and mitochondrial respiration increase lifespan.
source: In this context, increased metabolic activity and mitochondrial respiration increase lifespan (Speakman et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Speakman et al., 2004).

claim: Long-term caloric restriction and decreased metabolic rate reduce electron transport chain activity in the mitochondria and increase lifespan.
source: On the other hand, long-term caloric restriction and decreased metabolic rate reduce electron transport chain activity in the mitochondria and increase lifespan (Burkewitz et al., 2015; Durieux et al., 2011; Mattison et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Burkewitz et al., 2015; Durieux et al., 2011; Mattison et al., 2017).

claim: Caloric restriction increases lifespan in rats.
source: This paradoxical observation, first made in rats (McCay et al., 1935) and then extended to several species including C. elegans (Kimura et al., 1997; Lakowski and Hekimi, 1998) and primates (Mattison et al., 2017; Redman and Ravussin, 2011), argues for the opposite: that decreased metabolic and mitochondrial activity increases longevity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (McCay et al., 1935).

claim: Caloric restriction increases lifespan in C. elegans.
source: This paradoxical observation, first made in rats (McCay et al., 1935) and then extended to several species including C. elegans (Kimura et al., 1997; Lakowski and Hekimi, 1998) and primates (Mattison et al., 2017; Redman and Ravussin, 2011), argues for the opposite: that decreased metabolic and mitochondrial activity increases longevity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kimura et al., 1997; Lakowski and Hekimi, 1998).

claim: Caloric restriction increases lifespan in primates.
source: This paradoxical observation, first made in rats (McCay et al., 1935) and then extended to several species including C. elegans (Kimura et al., 1997; Lakowski and Hekimi, 1998) and primates (Mattison et al., 2017; Redman and Ravussin, 2011), argues for the opposite: that decreased metabolic and mitochondrial activity increases longevity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mattison et al., 2017; Redman and Ravussin, 2011).

claim: Loss of the insulin/insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) receptor daf-2 results in substantially increased adiposity and body fat stores with a concomitant increase in lifespan.
source: Loss of the insulin/insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) receptor daf-2, or of the transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) signal daf-7, each result in substantially increased adiposity and body fat stores, but with a concomitant increase in lifespan (Greer et al., 2008; Kimura et al., 1997; Ogg et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Greer et al., 2008; Kimura et al., 1997; Ogg et al., 1997).

claim: Loss of the transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) signal daf-7 results in substantially increased adiposity and body fat stores with a concomitant increase in lifespan.
source: Loss of the insulin/insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) receptor daf-2, or of the transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) signal daf-7, each result in substantially increased adiposity and body fat stores, but with a concomitant increase in lifespan (Greer et al., 2008; Kimura et al., 1997; Ogg et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Greer et al., 2008; Kimura et al., 1997; Ogg et al., 1997).

claim: There is a clear dissociation between fat storage and longevity amongst the various daf-2 alleles.
source: In the case of the DAF-2 insulin pathway, there is a clear dissociation between fat storage and longevity amongst the various daf-2 alleles (Perez and Van Gilst, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Perez and Van Gilst, 2008).

claim: Human observational studies repeatedly suggest either no relationship or an inverse association between adiposity and mortality in late life.
source: This non-linearity between adiposity and longevity is echoed in human observational studies that repeatedly suggest either no relationship (Kuk and Ardern, 2009; Reynolds et al., 2005), or an inverse association between adiposity and mortality in late life (Fontaine et al., 2003; Stevens et al., 1998; Zheng and Dirlam, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kuk and Ardern, 2009; Reynolds et al., 2005; Fontaine et al., 2003; Stevens et al., 1998; Zheng and Dirlam, 2016).

claim: The majority of C. elegans studies showing a relationship between reduced mitochondrial function and increased longevity come from manipulations that decrease fat oxidation and metabolic rate.
source: The majority of C. elegans studies showing a relationship between reduced mitochondrial function and increased longevity come from manipulations that decrease fat oxidation and metabolic rate (Dillin et al., 2002; Durieux et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dillin et al., 2002; Durieux et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2003).

claim: Serotonin is synthesized by the rate-limiting enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH-1) in only a few head neurons in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, 5-HT is synthesized by the rate-limiting enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH-1) in only a few head neurons (Sze et al., 2000) but has wide-ranging effects across the organism including lipid metabolism (Srinivasan et al., 2008), behavioral responses to food (Cunningham et al., 2012), reproduction (Tanis et al., 2008), and pathogen avoidance (Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Sze et al., 2000).

claim: Serotonin has wide-ranging effects across the C. elegans organism including lipid metabolism, behavioral responses to food, reproduction, and pathogen avoidance.
source: In C. elegans, 5-HT is synthesized by the rate-limiting enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH-1) in only a few head neurons (Sze et al., 2000) but has wide-ranging effects across the organism including lipid metabolism (Srinivasan et al., 2008), behavioral responses to food (Cunningham et al., 2012), reproduction (Tanis et al., 2008), and pathogen avoidance (Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Srinivasan et al., 2008; Cunningham et al., 2012; Tanis et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2005).

claim: Serotonin is a powerful stimulator of fat loss in the C. elegans intestine.
source: 5-HT is a powerful stimulator of fat loss in the intestine (Noble et al., 2013), wherein the majority of lipids are stored and metabolized (Srinivasan, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Noble et al., 2013; Srinivasan, 2015).

claim: Serotonin-elicited fat loss occurs by activating the mitochondrial beta-oxidation pathway.
source: 5-HT-elicited fat loss occurs by activating the mitochondrial beta-oxidation pathway (Srinivasan et al., 2008), in which stored triglyceride lipids are oxidized to usable energy (Salway, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Srinivasan et al., 2008; Salway, 1999).

claim: FLP-7 is the C. elegans ortholog of the mammalian family of tachykinin peptides.
source: FLP-7 is the C. elegans ortholog of the mammalian family of tachykinin peptides and is released from secretory neurons in response to fluctuations in neuronal 5-HTergic signaling.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: FLP-7 is released from secretory neurons in response to fluctuations in neuronal 5-HTergic signaling.
source: FLP-7 is the C. elegans ortholog of the mammalian family of tachykinin peptides and is released from secretory neurons in response to fluctuations in neuronal 5-HTergic signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' previous work as described in the manuscript.

claim: FLP-7 is secreted from the ASI neurons in which it is necessary and sufficient.
source: FLP-7 is secreted from the ASI neurons in which it is necessary and sufficient, and activates the G-protein-coupled receptor NPR-22 (ortholog of mammalian tachykinin receptor NK2R), in the intestinal cells (Palamiuc et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Palamiuc et al., 2017).

claim: FLP-7 activates the G-protein-coupled receptor NPR-22 in the intestinal cells.
source: FLP-7 is secreted from the ASI neurons in which it is necessary and sufficient, and activates the G-protein-coupled receptor NPR-22 (ortholog of mammalian tachykinin receptor NK2R), in the intestinal cells (Palamiuc et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Palamiuc et al., 2017).

claim: NPR-22 is the ortholog of mammalian tachykinin receptor NK2R.
source: FLP-7 is secreted from the ASI neurons in which it is necessary and sufficient, and activates the G-protein-coupled receptor NPR-22 (ortholog of mammalian tachykinin receptor NK2R), in the intestinal cells (Palamiuc et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Palamiuc et al., 2017).

claim: FLP-7/NPR-22 signaling transcriptionally activates the enzyme adipocyte triglyceride lipase (ATGL-1).
source: FLP-7/NPR-22 signaling transcriptionally activates the enzyme adipocyte triglyceride lipase (ATGL; ATGL-1 in C. elegans), a highly conserved lipolytic enzyme that regulates the first step in the fat oxidation and energy production cascade: the hydrolysis of triglycerides to free fatty acids.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' previous work as described in the manuscript.

claim: ATGL-1 is a highly conserved lipolytic enzyme that regulates the first step in the fat oxidation and energy production cascade: the hydrolysis of triglycerides to free fatty acids.
source: FLP-7/NPR-22 signaling transcriptionally activates the enzyme adipocyte triglyceride lipase (ATGL; ATGL-1 in C. elegans), a highly conserved lipolytic enzyme that regulates the first step in the fat oxidation and energy production cascade: the hydrolysis of triglycerides to free fatty acids.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: FLP-7/NPR-22 signaling does not alter behaviors or physiological outputs associated with global 5-HT signaling.
source: Critically, we previously showed that FLP-7/NPR-22 signaling does not alter behaviors or physiological outputs associated with global 5-HT signaling (Palamiuc et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Palamiuc et al., 2017).

claim: The FLP-7/NPR-22 tachykinin neuron-to-intestine signaling pathway is triggered by increases in neuronal 5-HT.
source: The FLP-7/NPR-22 tachykinin neuron-to-intestine signaling pathway is triggered by increases in neuronal 5-HT (Figure 1A–C), as previously published (Palamiuc et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Palamiuc et al., 2017) and by Figure 1A-C showing the pathway and FLP-7 secretion in response to 5-HT.

claim: flp-7tg worms have a significant reduction in intestinal fat stores.
source: First, we observed that flp-7tg worms have a significant reduction in intestinal fat stores (Figure 1D,E), recapitulating that seen with 5-HT treatment (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E demonstrating reduced fat content in flp-7tg animals.

claim: The fat reduction elicited by flp-7tg is dependent on the presence of the intestinal triglyceride lipase ATGL-1.
source: The fat reduction elicited by flp-7tg is dependent on the presence of the intestinal triglyceride lipase ATGL-1 (Figure 1D,E; note that the atgl-1 null mutant is inviable), as was noted for 5-HT itself (Figure 1F,G; Noble et al., 2013; Palamiuc et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E demonstrating that atgl-1 RNAi suppresses fat reduction in flp-7tg animals, and by citations to published literature (Noble et al., 2013; Palamiuc et al., 2017).

claim: FLP-7-stimulated fat loss is accompanied by increased basal and maximal respiration that are both abrogated upon RNAi-mediated inactivation of atgl-1.
source: Accordingly, FLP-7-stimulated fat loss is accompanied by increased basal and maximal respiration that are both abrogated upon RNAi-mediated inactivation of atgl-1 (Figure 1H,I), thus increased mitochondrial respiration in flp-7tg animals results from conversion of stored triglycerides to energy via beta-oxidation and ETC activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H,I demonstrating increased oxygen consumption rate in flp-7tg animals that is suppressed by atgl-1 RNAi.

claim: Increased mitochondrial respiration in flp-7tg animals results from conversion of stored triglycerides to energy via beta-oxidation and ETC activity.
source: Accordingly, FLP-7-stimulated fat loss is accompanied by increased basal and maximal respiration that are both abrogated upon RNAi-mediated inactivation of atgl-1 (Figure 1H,I), thus increased mitochondrial respiration in flp-7tg animals results from conversion of stored triglycerides to energy via beta-oxidation and ETC activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that atgl-1 RNAi suppresses both fat loss and increased respiration in flp-7tg animals.

claim: Behaviors elicited by 5-HT signaling including feeding rate, locomotion on and off food, and egg-laying remained unaltered in flp-7tg animals.
source: Finally, other behaviors elicited by 5-HT signaling including feeding rate (Figure 1J), locomotion on and off food (Figure 1K) and egg-laying (Figure 1L) remained unaltered in flp-7tg animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J-L demonstrating no significant differences in these behaviors between wild-type and flp-7tg animals.

claim: The flp-7tg line fully recapitulates the metabolic effects of genetic and pharmacological manipulation of neuronal 5-HT signaling without altering other 5-HT-mediated behaviors.
source: Thus, the flp-7tg line fully recapitulates the metabolic effects of genetic and pharmacological manipulation of neuronal 5-HT signaling without altering other 5-HT-mediated behaviors (Horvitz et al., 1982; Loer and Kenyon, 1993; Palamiuc et al., 2017; Song and Avery, 2012; Sze et al., 2000; Waggoner et al., 1998) and can serve as a valuable experimental handle to examine the long-term effects of sustained fat oxidation and increased ETC activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and by citations to published literature (Horvitz et al., 1982; Loer and Kenyon, 1993; Palamiuc et al., 2017; Song and Avery, 2012; Sze et al., 2000; Waggoner et al., 1998).

claim: Mild reductions in mitochondrial respiration can lead to a sustained increase in lifespan via decreased ROS production, hormesis, or other mechanisms.
source: Several lines of evidence have suggested that mild reductions in mitochondrial respiration can lead to a sustained increase in lifespan via decreased ROS production, hormesis, or other mechanisms (Braeckman et al., 1999; Copeland et al., 2009; Dell'agnello et al., 2007; Durieux et al., 2011; Feng et al., 2001; Yang and Hekimi, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Braeckman et al., 1999; Copeland et al., 2009; Dell'agnello et al., 2007; Durieux et al., 2011; Feng et al., 2001; Yang and Hekimi, 2010).

claim: flp-7tg animals had nearly the same lifespan as wild-type animals, with a non-significant difference (p=0.08 by Log-rank Test) in survival probability statistics.
source: However, we found that flp-7tg animals had nearly the same lifespan as wild-type animals, with a non-significant difference (p=0.08 by Log-rank Test) in survival probability statistics (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B demonstrating lifespan curves for wild-type and flp-7tg animals.

claim: In flp-7tg animals and in those treated with 5-HT, a two-fold induction of an integrated hsp-60::GFP transgene was observed, the canonical reporter for the mitochondrial stress response.
source: In the flp-7tg animals (Figure 2C–E) and in those treated with 5-HT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we observed a two-fold induction of an integrated hsp-60::GFP transgene, the canonical reporter for the mitochondrial stress response.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 demonstrating increased hsp-60 expression.

claim: Other stress responses including cytoplasmic heat-shock response (hsp-70 and hsp-16.2), oxidative stress (sod-3), nutrient stress (DAF-16 nuclear localization), and ER stress (hsp-4) were absent in flp-7tg animals.
source: Other stress responses were absent.
evidence: The claim is stated in the manuscript based on the authors' examination of various stress reporters.

claim: The induced mitochondrial hsp-60-mediated stress response was seen predominantly in the intestine.
source: The induced mitochondrial hsp-60-mediated stress response was seen predominantly in the intestine (Figure 2C) and was wholly dependent on the presence of atgl-1 because RNAi-mediated inactivation of atgl-1 ameliorated hsp-60 induction as judged by the reporter assay (Figure 2D) as well as by directly measuring hsp-60 transcripts by qPCR (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C demonstrating hsp-60::GFP expression in the intestine.

claim: The hsp-60-mediated stress response was wholly dependent on the presence of atgl-1.
source: The induced mitochondrial hsp-60-mediated stress response was seen predominantly in the intestine (Figure 2C) and was wholly dependent on the presence of atgl-1 because RNAi-mediated inactivation of atgl-1 ameliorated hsp-60 induction as judged by the reporter assay (Figure 2D) as well as by directly measuring hsp-60 transcripts by qPCR (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E demonstrating that atgl-1 RNAi suppresses hsp-60 induction.

claim: Fat oxidation evokes a mitochondrial stress response.
source: The increased mitochondrial respiration in flp-7tg also depended on atgl-1-dependent utilization of fat reserves (Figure 1H,I), suggesting the surprising result that fat oxidation evokes a mitochondrial stress response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that atgl-1-dependent fat oxidation is required for hsp-60 induction.

claim: All known mitochondrial stress pathways that induce hsp-60 require the mito-nuclear transcription factor called ATFS-1.
source: All known mitochondrial stress pathways that induce hsp-60 require the mito-nuclear transcription factor called ATFS-1 (Nargund et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Nargund et al., 2012).

claim: Under normal conditions, ATFS-1 is transported into mitochondria and degraded.
source: Under normal conditions, ATFS-1 is transported into mitochondria and degraded.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Under conditions that induce mitochondrial stress, ATFS-1 is stabilized and translocated to the nucleus where it initiates a range of transcriptional responses that allow adaptation to the stressor.
source: However, under conditions that induce mitochondrial stress, ATFS-1 is stabilized and translocated to the nucleus where it initiates a range of transcriptional responses that allow adaptation to the stressor (Lin and Haynes, 2016; Nargund et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Lin and Haynes, 2016; Nargund et al., 2015).

claim: hsp-60 was no longer induced by FLP-7 in the atfs-1(tm4525) null mutants.
source: As shown in Figure 2F and G, hsp-60 was no longer induced by FLP-7 in the atfs-1(tm4525) null mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F,G demonstrating that atfs-1 null mutants do not show hsp-60 induction in flp-7tg background.

claim: The combined loss of atgl-1 and atfs-1 completely suppressed the hsp-60 induction, which recapitulates the loss of each gene alone with no additive or synergistic effects.
source: We also noted that the combined loss of atgl-1 and atfs-1 completely suppressed the hsp-60 induction, which recapitulates the loss of each gene alone with no additive or synergistic effects (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F,G demonstrating that double loss of atgl-1 and atfs-1 does not further suppress hsp-60 induction compared to single loss.

claim: 5-HT-stimulated hsp-60 induction was completely suppressed with either atgl-1 or atfs-1 inactivation.
source: This finding was replicated with 5-HT-stimulated hsp-60 induction that was completely suppressed with either atgl-1 or atfs-1 inactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: atgl-1-dependent fat oxidation and atfs-1-dependent mitochondrial stress may function in a linear pathway.
source: This result suggested the possibility that atgl-1-dependent fat oxidation and atfs-1-dependent mitochondrial stress may function in a linear pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic epistasis data showing no additive effects of atgl-1 and atfs-1 loss.

claim: 5-HT-induced fat loss was partially suppressed in atfs-1 null mutants.
source: To our surprise, we found that 5-HT-induced fat loss was partially suppressed in atfs-1 null mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and FLP-7-induced fat loss was fully suppressed in atfs-1 null mutants (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: FLP-7-induced fat loss was fully suppressed in atfs-1 null mutants.
source: To our surprise, we found that 5-HT-induced fat loss was partially suppressed in atfs-1 null mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and FLP-7-induced fat loss was fully suppressed in atfs-1 null mutants (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B demonstrating that atfs-1 null mutants do not show fat loss in flp-7tg background.

claim: The absence of atfs-1 suppressed the transcriptional induction of atgl-1 by FLP-7 and 5-HT as judged by measuring the integrated atgl-1 reporter in vivo.
source: The absence of atfs-1 also suppressed the transcriptional induction of atgl-1 by FLP-7 and 5-HT as judged by measuring the integrated atgl-1 reporter in vivo (Figure 3C,D), and by direct measurement of atgl-1 transcripts by qPCR (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D demonstrating reduced atgl-1::GFP expression in atfs-1 null mutants.

claim: Loss of both atfs-1 and atgl-1 did not lead to a further suppression of FLP-7-induced fat loss.
source: As in the case of the hsp-60-mediated stress response (Figure 2D,E), loss of both atfs-1 and atgl-1 also did not lead to a further suppression of FLP-7-induced fat loss (Figure 3A,B), suggesting again that they function in a linear pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B demonstrating no additive effects of atfs-1 and atgl-1 loss on fat content.

claim: The effects of secreted FLP-7 on the intestine are intertwined: the mitochondrial stress response requires atgl-1 and fat oxidation, and fat oxidation requires the mito-nuclear stress response transcription factor atfs-1.
source: However, these data also indicated that the effects of secreted FLP-7 on the intestine are intertwined: on the one hand the mitochondrial stress response requires atgl-1 and fat oxidation (blue arrow; Figure 3F), and on the other hand fat oxidation requires the mito-nuclear stress response transcription factor atfs-1 (green arrow; Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing mutual dependence between atgl-1 and atfs-1 for their respective functions.

claim: Published ChIPseq and microarray studies of the ATFS-1 transcription factor did not suggest a direct induction of atgl-1 by ATFS-1.
source: Published ChIPseq and microarray studies of the ATFS-1 transcription factor did not suggest a direct induction of atgl-1 by ATFS-1 (Nargund et al., 2015; Nargund et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Nargund et al., 2015; Nargund et al., 2012).

claim: The putative cis-binding site of ATFS-1 was not found within a 5 kb region upstream of the atgl-1 transcriptional start site.
source: We also did not find the putative cis-binding site of ATFS-1 within a 5 kb region upstream of the atgl-1 transcriptional start site.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' analysis of the atgl-1 promoter sequence.

claim: ATFS-1 likely regulates atgl-1 transcription by an indirect mechanism.
source: Thus, ATFS-1 likely regulates atgl-1 transcription by an indirect mechanism.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of direct binding evidence and the requirement of ATFS-1 for atgl-1 induction.

claim: hlh-11 is the sole conserved ortholog of the mammalian transcription factor AP4.
source: Our top hit was a gene called hlh-11, the sole conserved ortholog of the mammalian transcription factor AP4 (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Lee et al., 2009).

claim: hlh-11(ok2944) null mutants showed significant in vivo induction of atgl-1 in the intestine.
source: We obtained and outcrossed a null mutant for hlh-11(ok2944), which when crossed into the Patgl-1::GFP reporter line showed significant in vivo induction of atgl-1 in the intestine (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B demonstrating increased atgl-1::GFP expression in hlh-11 null mutants.

claim: Transcript levels of atgl-1 mRNA were significantly greater in hlh-11 null mutants.
source: These results were reinforced by measuring transcript levels of atgl-1 mRNA by qPCR, which were significantly greater in hlh-11 null mutants (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C demonstrating increased atgl-1 mRNA in hlh-11 null mutants.

claim: The extent of atgl-1 induction by FLP-7 was matched by the absence of hlh-11, and without a further increase in flp-7tg;hlh-11 animals.
source: We also noted that the extent of atgl-1 induction by FLP-7 was matched by the absence of hlh-11, and without a further increase in flp-7tg;hlh-11 animals (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-C demonstrating no additive effects of flp-7tg and hlh-11 loss on atgl-1 expression.

claim: In wild-type animals, HLH-11 functions as a repressive transcription factor that suppresses atgl-1 under basal conditions.
source: These data suggested that in wild-type animals, HLH-11 functions as a repressive transcription factor that suppresses atgl-1 under basal conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased atgl-1 expression in hlh-11 null mutants.

claim: hlh-11 null mutants showed a dramatic ~70–80% decrease in body fat stores relative to wild-type.
source: hlh-11 null mutants showed a dramatic ~70–80% decrease in body fat stores relative to wild-type, and phenocopied the FLP-7 transgenic line (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D,E demonstrating reduced fat content in hlh-11 null mutants.

claim: flp-7tg;hlh-11 animals had significant reductions in body fat stores and resembled either single mutant alone.
source: flp-7tg;hlh-11 animals also had significant reductions in body fat stores and resembled either single mutant alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no additive effects of flp-7tg and hlh-11 loss on fat content.

claim: Removal of atgl-1 by RNAi completely suppressed fat loss in hlh-11 null mutants under all conditions.
source: Removal of atgl-1 by RNAi completely suppressed fat loss under all conditions (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D,E demonstrating that atgl-1 RNAi suppresses fat loss in hlh-11 null mutants.

claim: The fat loss phenotype of hlh-11 null mutants was accompanied by a significant increase in basal and maximal respiration that was also abrogated in the absence of atgl-1.
source: Further, the fat loss phenotype of hlh-11 null mutants was accompanied by a significant increase in basal and maximal respiration that was also abrogated in the absence of atgl-1 (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F,G demonstrating increased oxygen consumption rate in hlh-11 null mutants that is suppressed by atgl-1 RNAi.

claim: Loss of the transcription factor hlh-11 constitutively increases atgl-1 gene expression, fat oxidation, and energy expenditure.
source: Together, these data show that loss of the transcription factor hlh-11 constitutively increases atgl-1 gene expression, fat oxidation, and energy expenditure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased atgl-1 expression, reduced fat stores, and increased respiration in hlh-11 null mutants.

claim: HLH-11ox animals showed robust nuclear HLH-11 expression in the intestine.
source: We observed robust nuclear HLH-11 expression in the intestine (Figure 5A), suggesting a plausible model for the interaction between HLH-11 and atgl-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A demonstrating nuclear localization of HLH-11GFP in intestinal cells.

claim: HLH-11ox animals showed an ~40% increase in body fat stores compared to wild-type animals.
source: Remarkably, HLH-11ox animals showed an ~40% increase in body fat stores compared to wild-type animals and showed a near-complete suppression of the fat loss elicited in flp-7tg animals (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,C demonstrating increased fat content in HLH-11ox animals.

claim: HLH-11ox animals showed a near-complete suppression of the fat loss elicited in flp-7tg animals.
source: Remarkably, HLH-11ox animals showed an ~40% increase in body fat stores compared to wild-type animals and showed a near-complete suppression of the fat loss elicited in flp-7tg animals (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,C demonstrating that HLH-11 overexpression suppresses fat loss in flp-7tg animals.

claim: The increase in fat stores in HLH-11ox animals was accompanied by a corresponding decrease in maximal respiration, which was not further decreased upon removal of atgl-1.
source: The increase in fat stores was accompanied by a corresponding decrease in maximal respiration, which was not further decreased upon removal of atgl-1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D demonstrating decreased oxygen consumption rate in HLH-11ox animals.

claim: The fat accumulation and metabolic output in HLH-11ox and flp-7tg;HLH-11ox animals were accompanied by a significant decrease in atgl-1 mRNA.
source: The fat accumulation and metabolic output in HLH-11ox and flp-7tg;HLH-11ox animals were accompanied by a significant decrease in atgl-1 mRNA, as judged by qPCR (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E demonstrating decreased atgl-1 mRNA in HLH-11ox animals.

claim: HLH-11 plays an instructive role as a negative regulator of atgl-1 expression and influences fat oxidation and mitochondrial respiration in the intestine.
source: Thus, HLH-11 plays an instructive role as a negative regulator of atgl-1 expression and influences fat oxidation and mitochondrial respiration in the intestine.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that HLH-11 overexpression decreases atgl-1 expression, increases fat stores, and decreases respiration.

claim: Two HLH-11 cis-binding sites were identified at 891 and 2,386 bp upstream of the atgl-1 transcriptional start site.
source: We identified two HLH-11 cis-binding sites at 891 and 2,386 bp upstream of the atgl-1 transcriptional start site (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' analysis of the atgl-1 promoter sequence.

claim: HLH-11 is constitutively bound to the atgl-1 promoter under basal conditions.
source: Using three independent primer sets (Figure 5F), we observed atgl-1 promoter regions bound to HLH-11GFP in vehicle-treated animals, suggesting that HLH-11 is constitutively bound to the atgl-1 promoter under basal conditions (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G demonstrating HLH-11 binding to the atgl-1 promoter by ChIP-qPCR.

claim: 5-HT treatment significantly reduced atgl-1 promoter occupancy by HLH-11 relative to vehicle treated animals.
source: Importantly, 5-HT treatment significantly reduced atgl-1 promoter occupancy by HLH-11 relative to vehicle treated animals (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G demonstrating reduced HLH-11 binding to the atgl-1 promoter after 5-HT treatment by ChIP-qPCR.

claim: The transcription factor HLH-11 binds directly to the atgl-1 promoter, and 5-HT signaling diminishes this interaction, ultimately promoting fat loss.
source: Thus, the transcription factor HLH-11 binds directly to the atgl-1 promoter, and 5-HT signaling diminishes this interaction, ultimately promoting fat loss.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the ChIP-qPCR data showing direct binding of HLH-11 to the atgl-1 promoter and reduced binding after 5-HT treatment.

claim: An extrachromosomal atgl-1 reporter line that lacked both hlh-11 cis sites showed an ~2-fold increase in atgl-1 expression.
source: Finally, we generated an extrachromosomal atgl-1 reporter line that lacked both hlh-11 cis sites (Δcishlh-11) and observed an ~2-fold increase in atgl-1 expression (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H,I demonstrating increased atgl-1::GFP expression in the reporter lacking HLH-11 binding sites.

claim: The conserved transcription factor HLH-11 is a direct repressor of atgl-1 expression, fat loss, and mitochondrial respiration.
source: Taken together, the conserved transcription factor HLH-11 is a direct repressor of atgl-1 expression, fat loss, and mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing direct binding of HLH-11 to the atgl-1 promoter and the effects of HLH-11 loss and overexpression on atgl-1 expression, fat content, and respiration.

claim: The flp-7tg line had reduced HLH-11GFP in the nuclei of the intestinal cells relative to wild-type.
source: We found that relative to wild-type, the flp-7tg line had reduced HLH-11GFP in the nuclei of the intestinal cells (Figure 6A,B), suggesting that hlh-11 is downregulated by secreted FLP-7.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B demonstrating reduced HLH-11GFP fluorescence in flp-7tg animals.

claim: hlh-11 is downregulated by secreted FLP-7.
source: We found that relative to wild-type, the flp-7tg line had reduced HLH-11GFP in the nuclei of the intestinal cells (Figure 6A,B), suggesting that hlh-11 is downregulated by secreted FLP-7.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced HLH-11 expression in flp-7tg animals.

claim: hlh-11 transcripts were reduced in flp-7tg animals as measured by qPCR.
source: This observation was corroborated by measuring hlh-11 transcripts using qPCR (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C demonstrating reduced hlh-11 mRNA in flp-7tg animals.

claim: Neuronally-secreted FLP-7 negatively regulates intestinal HLH-11 that directly binds to and represses ATGL-1 transcription.
source: These experiments establish that neuronally-secreted FLP-7 negatively regulates intestinal HLH-11 that directly binds to and represses ATGL-1 transcription.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that FLP-7 reduces HLH-11 expression and that HLH-11 directly binds to and represses atgl-1.

claim: A previous report had listed hlh-11 as one of the direct targets of ATFS-1.
source: In seeking a greater understanding of how ATFS-1 may be connected to HLH-11, we serendipitously found that a previous report had listed hlh-11 as one of the direct targets of ATFS-1 (Nargund et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Nargund et al., 2015).

claim: atfs-1 removal blunted FLP-7-mediated hlh-11 repression.
source: We found that atfs-1 removal blunted FLP-7-mediated hlh-11 repression (Figure 6C), suggesting that FLP-7-mediated hlh-11 repression requires atfs-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C demonstrating that atfs-1 null mutants do not show hlh-11 repression in flp-7tg background.

claim: In flp-7tg animals, inactivation of atgl-1 blunted hlh-11 repression.
source: In flp-7tg animals, inactivation of atgl-1, a condition that would simultaneously block fat oxidation and atfs-1 activation, also blunted this hlh-11 repression, suggesting a connection between fat oxidation, atfs-1 induction, and hlh-11 repression.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that atgl-1 RNAi blunts hlh-11 repression in flp-7tg animals.

claim: Loss of both atfs-1 and atgl-1 diminished the FLP-7-dependent suppression of hlh-11 to a similar extent as loss of either gene alone.
source: Loss of both atfs-1 and atgl-1 diminished the FLP-7-dependent suppression of hlh-11 to a similar extent as loss of either gene alone (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C demonstrating no additive effects of atfs-1 and atgl-1 loss on hlh-11 expression.

claim: A feedback loop exists where repression of hlh-11 by FLP-7 permits atgl-1-dependent fat oxidation, which induces atfs-1 and in turn represses hlh-11 to sustain and augment fat oxidation.
source: These results suggest the interesting possibility of a feedback loop (Figure 6D): repression of hlh-11 by FLP-7 permits atgl-1-dependent fat oxidation, which induces atfs-1 and in turn represses hlh-11 to sustain and augment fat oxidation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the relationships between FLP-7, HLH-11, ATGL-1, and ATFS-1.

claim: HLH-11 overexpression, which represses atgl-1 mRNA, showed a significant decrease in hsp-60 mRNA.
source: Accordingly, we found that overexpression of HLH-11, which represses atgl-1 mRNA (Figure 5E), showed a significant decrease in hsp-60 mRNA (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating decreased hsp-60 mRNA in HLH-11ox animals.

claim: HLH-11ox decreases not only fat loss and mitochondrial respiration, but also the ensuing stress response.
source: Thus, HLH-11ox decreases not only fat loss and mitochondrial respiration (Figure 5B,C,D), but also the ensuing stress response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that HLH-11 overexpression decreases fat loss, respiration, and hsp-60 expression.

claim: hlh-11 null mutants significantly increased hsp-60 mRNA.
source: In contrast, hlh-11 null mutants, which constitutively stimulate fat oxidation and mitochondrial respiration by modulating atgl-1 transcription (Figure 4), significantly increased hsp-60 mRNA (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating increased hsp-60 mRNA in hlh-11 null mutants.

claim: Effects of HLH-11 overexpression and absence were identical in the presence and absence of FLP-7 secretion.
source: Effects of HLH-11 overexpression and absence were identical in the presence and absence of FLP-7 secretion (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating similar effects of HLH-11 manipulation in wild-type and flp-7tg backgrounds.

claim: The induction of hsp-60 upon loss of hlh-11 was fully suppressed by removal of either atgl-1, atfs-1, or both.
source: Also, the induction of hsp-60 upon loss of hlh-11 was fully suppressed by removal of either atgl-1, atfs-1, or both, suggesting that HLH-11 mediated mitochondrial stress is a direct consequence of fat oxidation (Figures 2F,G and 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating that atgl-1 or atfs-1 RNAi suppresses hsp-60 induction in hlh-11 null mutants.

claim: HLH-11 mediated mitochondrial stress is a direct consequence of fat oxidation.
source: Also, the induction of hsp-60 upon loss of hlh-11 was fully suppressed by removal of either atgl-1, atfs-1, or both, suggesting that HLH-11 mediated mitochondrial stress is a direct consequence of fat oxidation (Figures 2F,G and 7A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that the mitochondrial stress response in hlh-11 mutants requires atgl-1 and atfs-1.

claim: hlh-11 mutants increased atgl-1 expression with and without increased FLP-7 secretion as judged by atgl-1 reporter expression and qPCR.
source: As expected, hlh-11 mutants increased atgl-1 expression with and without increased FLP-7 secretion as judged by atgl-1 reporter expression (Figure 7B,C) as well as qPCR (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B-D demonstrating increased atgl-1 expression in hlh-11 null mutants.

claim: atfs-1 loss alone does not lead to appreciable changes in atgl-1.
source: Also as predicted, atfs-1 loss alone does not lead to appreciable changes in atgl-1 (Figure 7B–D); this is because atfs-1 is non-functional in wild-type animals (Nargund et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B-D and by a citation to published literature (Nargund et al., 2012).

claim: hlh-11;atfs-1 double mutants resembled hlh-11 mutants alone.
source: In contrast, hlh-11;atfs-1 double mutants resembled hlh-11 mutants alone, thus during increased FLP-7 secretion, atfs-1-dependent induction of atgl-1 requires hlh-11 repression (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B-D demonstrating no additive effects of hlh-11 and atfs-1 loss on atgl-1 expression.

claim: During increased FLP-7 secretion, atfs-1-dependent induction of atgl-1 requires hlh-11 repression.
source: In contrast, hlh-11;atfs-1 double mutants resembled hlh-11 mutants alone, thus during increased FLP-7 secretion, atfs-1-dependent induction of atgl-1 requires hlh-11 repression (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic epistasis data showing that hlh-11;atfs-1 double mutants resemble hlh-11 single mutants.

claim: In the context of flp-7tg animals, hlh-11 mutants show augmented fat loss, whereas atfs-1 removal blocked reduced fat stores.
source: flp-7tg animals have reduced fat stores because of increased atgl-1-dependent fat oxidation (Figure 1). In the context of flp-7tg animals, hlh-11 mutants also show augmented fat loss, whereas atfs-1 removal blocked reduced fat stores (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A,B demonstrating the effects of hlh-11 and atfs-1 mutations on fat content in flp-7tg background.

claim: hlh-11;atfs-1 double mutants resembled hlh-11 single mutants alone in their fat phenotypes.
source: In accordance with the increased atgl-1 transcript levels (Figure 7B–D), we found that hlh-11;atfs-1 double mutants also resembled hlh-11 single mutants alone in their fat phenotypes, suggesting that the suppression of fat oxidation in atfs-1 mutants is dependent on the presence of hlh-11 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 demonstrating similar fat content in hlh-11 and hlh-11;atfs-1 mutants.

claim: The suppression of fat oxidation in atfs-1 mutants is dependent on the presence of hlh-11.
source: In accordance with the increased atgl-1 transcript levels (Figure 7B–D), we found that hlh-11;atfs-1 double mutants also resembled hlh-11 single mutants alone in their fat phenotypes, suggesting that the suppression of fat oxidation in atfs-1 mutants is dependent on the presence of hlh-11 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic epistasis data showing that hlh-11;atfs-1 double mutants resemble hlh-11 single mutants.

claim: In the presence of increased FLP-7 secretion, hlh-11;atfs-1 double mutants showed a slight but significant augmentation of fat loss relative to flp-7tg animals alone.
source: We note that in the presence of increased FLP-7 secretion, hlh-11;atfs-1 double mutants showed a slight but significant augmentation of fat loss relative to flp-7tg animals alone (Figure 8A,B); it is possible that of the hundreds of ATFS-1 targets, genes in addition to HLH-11 may play a role.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A,B demonstrating slightly increased fat loss in flp-7tg;hlh-11;atfs-1 animals compared to flp-7tg alone.

claim: ATFS-1-dependent fat oxidation requires hlh-11 repression of atgl-1.
source: Thus, ATFS-1-dependent fat oxidation requires hlh-11 repression of atgl-1 (Figure 8A,B); HLH-11 acts genetically downstream of ATFS-1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic epistasis data showing that hlh-11 loss suppresses the effects of atfs-1 loss on fat oxidation.

claim: HLH-11 acts genetically downstream of ATFS-1.
source: Thus, ATFS-1-dependent fat oxidation requires hlh-11 repression of atgl-1 (Figure 8A,B); HLH-11 acts genetically downstream of ATFS-1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic epistasis data showing that hlh-11 loss suppresses the effects of atfs-1 loss.

claim: In flp-7tg animals removal of both hlh-11 and atfs-1 led to a significant decrease in both median and maximal lifespan (p<0.001).
source: In testing this idea, we found that in flp-7tg animals removal of both hlh-11 and atfs-1 led to a significant decrease in both median and maximal lifespan (p<0.001, Figure 8C,F) that was not seen in hlh-11;atfs-1 mutants (Figure 8D), hlh-11 (Figure 8E) or atfs-1 mutants (Tian et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C,F demonstrating decreased lifespan in flp-7tg;hlh-11;atfs-1 animals.

claim: The decrease in lifespan was not seen in hlh-11;atfs-1 mutants, hlh-11 mutants, or atfs-1 mutants alone.
source: In testing this idea, we found that in flp-7tg animals removal of both hlh-11 and atfs-1 led to a significant decrease in both median and maximal lifespan (p<0.001, Figure 8C,F) that was not seen in hlh-11;atfs-1 mutants (Figure 8D), hlh-11 (Figure 8E) or atfs-1 mutants (Tian et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D,E and by a citation to published literature (Tian et al., 2016).

claim: In hlh-11;atfs-1 mutants alone (without increased FLP-7 secretion) modest fat loss was observed that is not sufficient to shift lifespan in either direction.
source: We reasoned that in hlh-11;atfs-1 mutants alone (that is, without increased FLP-7 secretion) we observed modest fat loss (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) that is not sufficient to shift lifespan in either direction (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing modest fat loss and normal lifespan in hlh-11;atfs-1 mutants.

claim: Even though hlh-11 mutants show a substantial increase in fat oxidation, the presence of atfs-1 prevents lifespan shortening.
source: Even though hlh-11 mutants show a substantial increase in fat oxidation (Figure 4D,E), the presence of atfs-1 (Figure 8E) prevents lifespan shortening.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that hlh-11 mutants have normal lifespan despite increased fat oxidation.

claim: FLP-7 secretion serves as the neuronal cue to trigger fat oxidation by repressing hlh-11 expression, that in turn de-represses atgl-1.
source: Our data and model (Figure 8G) are consistent with the following interpretation: FLP-7 secretion serves as the neuronal cue to trigger fat oxidation by repressing hlh-11 expression, that in turn de-represses atgl-1 (red pathway, Figure 8G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the pathway from FLP-7 to HLH-11 to ATGL-1.

claim: The increase in fat oxidation and mitochondrial respiration generates an ATFS-1-mediated mitochondrial response, as judged by induction of the mitochondrial stress sensor hsp-60.
source: The resulting increase in fat oxidation and mitochondrial respiration generates an ATFS-1-mediated mitochondrial response, as judged by induction of the mitochondrial stress sensor hsp-60.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that fat oxidation induces hsp-60 in an ATFS-1-dependent manner.

claim: ATFS-1 induction serves as a second cue from the mitochondria to further repress hlh-11, which in turn augments fat oxidation via ATGL-1 in a feedback loop.
source: We propose that ATFS-1 induction serves as a second cue from the mitochondria to further repress hlh-11, which in turn augments fat oxidation via ATGL-1 in a feedback loop (green pathway, Figure 8G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the feedback relationship between ATFS-1 and HLH-11.

claim: The atgl-1/atfs-1/hlh-11 feedback loop serves the dual functions of sustaining fat oxidation and protecting lifespan.
source: The atgl-1/atfs-1/hlh-11 feedback loop serves the dual functions of sustaining fat oxidation and protecting lifespan.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that disruption of the feedback loop leads to decreased lifespan in the context of increased fat oxidation.

claim: The hlh-11/atgl-1 arm of the pathway primarily drives fat loss, whereas the atfs-1/hlh-11 arm of the pathway primarily protects lifespan.
source: Although each influences the other, the hlh-11/atgl-1 arm of the pathway primarily drives fat loss, whereas the atfs-1/hlh-11 arm of the pathway primarily protects lifespan.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing differential effects of manipulating different components of the pathway on fat loss versus lifespan.

claim: Sustained fat oxidation evokes a mitochondrial stress response that functions to simultaneously augment fat oxidation and confer longevity protection.
source: We report here that sustained fat oxidation evokes a mitochondrial stress response that functions to simultaneously augment fat oxidation and confer longevity protection (modeled in Figure 8G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the feedback loop between fat oxidation and mitochondrial stress response, and the effects on lifespan.

claim: The dual control of fat oxidation and lifespan protection emerges from a feedback transcriptional loop that shields the organism from life-shortening mitochondrial stress in the face of continuous fat oxidation.
source: We have found that the dual control of fat oxidation and lifespan protection emerges from a feedback transcriptional loop that shields the organism from life-shortening mitochondrial stress in the face of continuous fat oxidation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the feedback loop and its effects on fat oxidation and lifespan.

claim: Sustained fat oxidation does not shorten lifespan because a mitochondrial response protects both.
source: Thus, sustained fat oxidation does not shorten lifespan because a mitochondrial response protects both.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that flp-7tg animals with increased fat oxidation have normal lifespan, but disruption of the mitochondrial stress response leads to shortened lifespan.

claim: Under normal or wild-type conditions when fat oxidation levels are not high, the feedback loop remains latent.
source: Under normal or wild-type conditions when fat oxidation levels are not high, this loop remains latent.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that the feedback loop is activated under conditions of increased fat oxidation.

claim: Under conditions in which mitochondrial function is not compromised, the dissociation between adiposity and longevity may be broadly conserved.
source: We speculate that under conditions in which mitochondrial function is not compromised, the dissociation between adiposity and longevity may be broadly conserved.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the authors' interpretation of their findings.

claim: The conserved transcription factor HLH-11 functions as the nexus of the signaling pathway and receives two signals: one non-cell-autonomous via neuronal FLP-7 and the other cell-autonomous via the mito-nuclear transcription factor, ATFS-1.
source: The conserved transcription factor HLH-11 functions as the nexus of this signaling pathway and receives two signals: one non-cell-autonomous via neuronal FLP-7 that transmits sensory signals to initiate a metabolic response, and the other cell-autonomous via the mito-nuclear transcription factor, ATFS-1, that coordinates the mitochondrial stress response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that HLH-11 is regulated by both FLP-7 and ATFS-1.

claim: The mammalian ortholog of HLH-11, called AP4, is widely distributed along the epithelial cells of the mammalian intestine, as is ATGL.
source: Interestingly, the mammalian ortholog of HLH-11, called AP4, is widely distributed along the epithelial cells of the mammalian intestine, as is ATGL (Jung and Hermeking, 2009; Obrowsky et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Jung and Hermeking, 2009; Obrowsky et al., 2013).

claim: Sustained β-oxidation via activation of the conserved triglyceride lipase ATGL-1 triggers a feedback transcriptional loop that involves the mito-nuclear transcription factor ATFS-1 and a previously unknown and highly conserved repressor of ATGL-1 called HLH-11/AP4.
source: We find that sustained β-oxidation via activation of the conserved triglyceride lipase ATGL-1, triggers a feedback transcriptional loop that involves the mito-nuclear transcription factor ATFS-1, and a previously unknown and highly conserved repressor of ATGL-1 called HLH-11/AP4.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript demonstrating the feedback loop between ATGL-1, ATFS-1, and HLH-11.

claim: This feedback loop orchestrates the dual control of fat oxidation and lifespan, and shields the organism from life-shortening mitochondrial stress in the face of continuous fat oxidation.
source: This feedback loop orchestrates the dual control of fat oxidation and lifespan, and shields the organism from life-shortening mitochondrial stress in the face of continuous fat oxidation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing that the feedback loop regulates both fat oxidation and lifespan, and that disruption of the loop leads to shortened lifespan under conditions of increased fat oxidation.
